questions.prompt: In a medical test, $P(+\mid \text{sick})=0.9$ and $P(\text{sick})=0.01$. What **can't** you compute without more information?
questions.model_answer: $P(\text{sick}\mid +)$, because $P(+\mid\text{healthy})$ is missing, so $P(+)$ can't be computed.
questions.explanation: The other three follow directly from the data. Reversing the condition (Bayes) needs $P(+)$, and for that the false-positive rate is missing.

questions.prompt: Roll a fair die. $A$ = "an even number", $B$ = "a number greater than 3". What is $P(A\mid B)$?
questions.explanation: Restrict the sample space to $B=\{4,5,6\}$; two of those are even.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what is the difference between disjoint events and independent events? Give an example.
questions.model_answer: Disjoint: they can't happen together ($P(A\cap B)=0$). Independent: knowing one doesn't change the probability of the other ($P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$). Disjoint events with positive probability are always dependent.
questions.explanation: A common mistake: disjointness is about an empty intersection, independence is about probabilities.

questions.prompt: A random variable $X$ is 1 with probability $p$ and 0 otherwise. What is $E[X]$?
questions.explanation: The expectation is the average of the values, weighted by their probabilities.
